Drive-in
DRYV-in
noun (Silent Generation slang)
The first drive-in movie theater opened in Camden, New Jersey, in 1933; drive-in restaurants, where carhops brought trays to the window, had spread through the South and West in the 1920s and 1930s. The word drive-in named both. After the war the outdoor theaters multiplied across the country, and by the 1950s the drive-in — the big screen, the window speaker, the snack bar — was the Saturday night of the Silent Generation and their young families.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To Grandma and Grandpa, drive-in meant two things. On a hot afternoon it meant the burger stand where a carhop brought a tray to hook on the car window. On Saturday night it meant the movie lot outside town: a hundred cars facing a giant screen, a tinny speaker on the window, the kids in pajamas in the back seat, and a paper sack of popcorn passed around. Families went together; courting couples went too. It was simple, cheap, and happy, and there is much to bless in it. The early church ate together "with gladness and singleness of heart" (Act 2:46), and a family sharing a meal and a story under the stars is a small echo of that. But the drive-in also put a screen in front of young eyes, and some of the screens and some of the back rows were not clean. David’s resolve is worth teaching: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3). Our Lord said, "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Mat 6:22). And Paul gives a filter for every screen we will ever sit before: "whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely…think on these things" (Php 4:8). Christ is the light every story should lead us toward; a family that watches with that filter can still enjoy a good picture under the stars.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation word (1930s coinage; 1950s heyday) for the outdoor car movie theater and the carhop burger stand — a place of family gladness, and a reminder to set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psa 101:3).

expand to see more

DRIVE-IN, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1930s–50s) An outdoor movie theater where patrons watch from their cars; also a restaurant serving customers in their cars. "Dad piled us in the station wagon in our pajamas and took us to the drive-in."

Webster (1828) — DRIVE, verb transitive preterit tense Drove, [formerly drave; participle passive Driven, G.] 1. To impel or urge forward by force; to force; to move by physical force. We drive a nail into wood with a hammer; the wind or a current drive a ship on the ocean. 4. To impel a team of horses or oxen to move forward, and to direct their course; hence, to guide or regulate the course of the carriage drawn by them. We say, to drive a team, or to drive a carriage drawn by a team.

Decode for families: what the drive-in shows is the question; the screen in your pocket is the drive-in now.

Key Scripture

Act 2:46 — "And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,"

Psa 101:3 — "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me."

Mat 6:22 — "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light."

Php 4:8 — "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things."

Modern Corruption

A wholesome place-word, though the drive-in theater’s back rows earned a reputation, and its screens brought both clean and unclean pictures before young eyes.

expand to see more

Most of what drive-in remembers is good: a cheap family night, a burger brought to the window, neighbours parked side by side. Nothing in the word needs correcting.

Honesty requires one gentle note. Teenagers of the 1950s gave the drive-in theater a less innocent nickname, because a parked car in the dark was a temptation to courting couples, and the films grew less clean as the years went on. The wisdom of Job and David applies to the back seat and the screen alike: make a covenant with the eyes (Job 31:1) and set no wicked thing before them (Psa 101:3).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English drifan (to drive, urge on) + in → drive-in restaurant (1920s–30s) → drive-in theater (1933) → 1950s Saturday-night institution.

expand to see more

Old English drifan — to drive, urge on, compel

1920s–30s: drive-in restaurants with carhops at the window

1933: the first drive-in movie theater, Camden, New Jersey

1950s: outdoor screens across the country; the family Saturday night

Today: a nostalgic word, and a few surviving screens

Usage

""We saw every Disney picture at the drive-in with you kids asleep in the back by the second reel.""

"I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psa 101:3)."

"The light of the body is the eye (Mat 6:22)."
